title: Dracula
author: Bram Stoker
about:
A young English solicitor travels to Transylvania to help Count Dracula buy an English property. His business diary gradually becomes the record of a captivity he cannot explain. In England, letters between Mina Murray and Lucy Westenra introduce another circle of lives, soon drawn into the same danger. Doctors, friends and lovers must decide what to believe, whom to trust, and how to act when familiar explanations fail.

Published in 1897, Bram Stoker’s novel tells its story through journals, letters, telegrams, newspaper reports and recorded testimony. No single narrator sees everything. The characters assemble and compare their accounts, making the reader both a witness to their fear and a fellow investigator. Trains, shorthand, typewriters and phonographs share the page with castles, crucifixes and beliefs the investigators would once have dismissed.

whyItMatters.title: Evidence needs other people
whyItMatters.body: Jonathan’s diary, Seward’s recordings and Mina’s transcriptions gain force when they are brought together. The novel makes cooperation a practical matter: a detail that means little to one witness can change another person’s understanding. It also asks what protection is lost when people withhold information from someone they love.

whyItMatters.title: Care can become control
whyItMatters.body: The effort to protect Lucy and Mina brings tenderness, medical intervention and decisions made on their behalf. Following who speaks, who is believed and who is excluded reveals the tension between helping a person and taking away her authority over her own life.

whyItMatters.title: The familiar world can carry the threat
whyItMatters.body: Dracula’s plans depend on ordinary arrangements: buying property, shipping cargo, taking trains and sending letters. The danger travels through systems that promise order and connection. Reading those practical details closely makes the supernatural threat more unsettling, because it uses the same world as everyone else.

angleCards.title: Read the dates and the documents
angleCards.text: Notice who records each entry, when it was written and when another person can read it. A telegram’s delay or a diary kept private can matter as much as a dramatic encounter.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to follow how the dated documents distribute knowledge, and how delays and gaps change what the characters can do.

angleCards.title: Listen for different voices
angleCards.text: Jonathan begins as an observant traveller, Mina as an organised and attentive correspondent, Lucy as an intimate and playful friend, and Seward as a doctor studying a case. Listen to how their habits of expression change under pressure, and how Van Helsing’s distinctive English combines reasoning with urgency.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to compare the narrators’ voices and notice what their different ways of speaking reveal about their fears and assumptions.

angleCards.title: Track the work of care
angleCards.text: Pay attention to nursing, sleepless watches, transcription and emotional reassurance. Then ask who decides what counts as protection, and whether the person being protected gets a say.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to read for the practical and emotional work of care, including its unequal distribution and its limits.

angleCards.title: Watch modern tools meet old beliefs
angleCards.text: Keep a mental list of the devices, timetables, medical practices and religious objects the characters use. Notice when a confident explanation stops working, and what makes someone accept a different kind of evidence.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to examine how scientific habits, modern technology and religious belief interact in the investigation.

cast.name: Jonathan Harker
cast.description: A newly qualified English solicitor sent to complete a property transaction with Count Dracula. His shorthand journal opens the novel, recording travel details before his professional visit becomes frightening.

cast.name: Mina Murray / Mina Harker
cast.description: Jonathan’s fiancée and Lucy’s close friend. She practises shorthand and typing, pays close attention to other people, and becomes essential to assembling the scattered records. Her surname changes after marriage.

cast.name: Count Dracula
cast.description: A Transylvanian nobleman preparing to move to England. His formal hospitality, knowledge of English life and pride in his ancestry conceal purposes Jonathan cannot at first understand.

cast.name: Lucy Westenra
cast.description: A young woman whose lively letters tell Mina about love and courtship. Her relationships bring Arthur Holmwood, John Seward and Quincey Morris into the story.

cast.name: Dr. John Seward
cast.role: The doctor who records his observations
cast.description: A physician in charge of a private asylum and one of Lucy’s suitors. His phonograph diary mixes clinical investigation with feelings he cannot easily keep apart from his work.

cast.name: Professor Abraham Van Helsing
cast.description: A learned doctor from Amsterdam whom Seward calls upon for help. His distinctive English and willingness to consider unfamiliar explanations make him an unusual guide for the group.

cast.name: Arthur Holmwood / Lord Godalming
cast.description: The man Lucy loves, and a friend of Seward and Quincey Morris. He later inherits the title Lord Godalming; the two names refer to the same man after that change.

cast.name: Quincey P. Morris
cast.description: An American traveller and another of Lucy’s suitors. His playful speech gives way to directness when events demand it, and friendship matters to him even after disappointment.

cast.name: R. M. Renfield
cast.description: A patient whose behaviour fascinates and unsettles Seward. Much of what the reader first hears about him comes through the doctor’s observations, a perspective worth questioning.

openingText: 3 May. Bistritz.—I left Munich at 8:35 P. M. on 1 May and reached Vienna early the following morning. We were due at 6:46, but the train arrived an hour late. From what I could see through the train window, and during my short walk through its streets, Buda-Pesth looks a wonderful place. I dared not venture far from the station: we had arrived late, and the train would leave as close to its proper time as it could. I had the feeling that we were leaving the West behind and entering the East. The westernmost of the magnificent bridges across the Danube, a river impressively wide and deep here, carried us into a world shaped by the traditions of Turkish rule.
